### Load packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
source("99_my_transpose.R")
```

### Loading output data from 01_load



```{r, warning=FALSE}
# Load datasets into environment
data_path = "../data/"

pam50 <- read_tsv(str_c(data_path, "01_dat_load_pam50.tsv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)
proteomes  <- read_tsv(str_c(data_path, "01_dat_load_proteomes.tsv"),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)
clinical <- read_tsv(str_c(data_path, "01_dat_load_clinical.tsv"),
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
head(proteomes)
```

### Duplicate samples

For three of the patients, duplicate samples were collected. First we check the correlation between duplicate samples to be sure that duplicates from the same patient are consistent.

```{r}
# Extraxt all the sample cols
sample_cols <- proteomes |> 
  select(ends_with("TCGA"))

# Extract all the duplicate pairs of the patient ID
duplicate_columns <- tibble(full_id = names(sample_cols)) |> 
  mutate(patient_id = str_sub(full_id, 1 , 7)) |> 
  filter(n() > 1, .by = patient_id) |> 
  pull(patient_id)

# Now display the correlation between the pair
correlation_matrix <- sample_cols |> 
  select(starts_with(duplicate_columns)) |> 
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")


correlation_matrix
```

The duplicates are located by first 7 characters of each patient. Here we find that the duplicates A0-A12D, C8-A131 and A0-A12B are all positively correlated pairwise, so we decide to merge them.

#### Mean duplicate protein expression levels

We merge the duplicates so that each patient has only one measured protein expression level pr. protein. We do this by taking the mean between the two duplicate samples, seeing as the three duplicates correlate well.

```{r}
head(proteomes)
```

```{r}
proteomes_dupmean <- proteomes |> 
  # Pivot longer only keeping 
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(RefSeq_accession_number, gene_symbol,gene_name),
               names_to = "ID",
               values_to = "log2_ratio") |> 
  
  # Changeing patient id's to get a shared column with the pam50 dataset
  mutate(patient_id = if_else(str_ends(ID, "TCGA"),
                              # Change the order of the ID so TCGA is first and the other substring after
                              str_c("TCGA-", str_sub(ID, 1, 7)),
                              ID)) |> 

  # Locating duplicates for all the transcripts by grouping using the accession number and the ID. 
  group_by(RefSeq_accession_number, ID) |> 
  # Calculate the average log2_ratio for all the groups (duplicates). If one of the replicate contains NA use the other value
  summarise(log2_ratio = mean(log2_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |> 
  
  # Pivot wide to get ID's back as columns
  pivot_wider(names_from = ID,
              values_from = log2_ratio)

```

```{r}
proteomes_dupmean
```

### Renaming columns of the PAM50 file before merging

The columns in the PAM50 dataset have a slightly different naming convention:

```{r}
head(pam50)
```

In order to filter the proteomic dataset down to only the PAM50 gene reference list, we rename RefSeqProteinID to RefSeq_accession_number in the PAM50 table to get a common column name.

```{r}
pam50 <- pam50 |>
  rename(RefSeq_accession_number = RefSeqProteinID)
```

### Merge data

#### Proteomes for only PAM50 genes

The PAM50 dataset contains genes, whose mRNA expression signatures can be used to classify breast cancer into 5 different subtypes. To compare classification by mRNA expression (assigned labels in clinical data) vs protein expression for these genes, we merge these two datasets, keeping only the expression profiles of PAM50 proteins for our study.

```{r}
# left joins to only keep the 100 reference genes for breast cancer
proteomes_pam50_joined <-  inner_join(pam50,
                                      proteomes_dupmean,
                                      by = "RefSeq_accession_number"
                                      )

head(proteomes_pam50_joined)
```

#### Entire proteomes dataset merged with the clinical dataset

In order to utilise the clinical data for each patient, such as the RNA PAM50 classification of breast cancer subtypes, in our analysis, we join the proteomic data to the clinical dataset. As the clinical data has patient IDs in a column, we transpose the proteomic data:

```{r}
proteomes_dupmean_transposed <- my_transpose(proteomes_dupmean)

head(proteomes_dupmean_transposed)
```

We can now join by the common column 'patient_id', called 'Complete TCGA ID' in the clinical dataset:

```{r}
final_dataset_all_genes <- left_join(proteomes_dupmean_transposed,
                                     clinical,
                                     by = c("patient_id" = "Complete TCGA ID")
                                     )

head(final_dataset_all_genes)
```

#### PAM50 filtered proteomes merged with clinical data

```{r}
proteomes_pam50_transposed <- my_transpose(proteomes_pam50_joined)

head(proteomes_pam50_transposed)
```

left_join(), creating NA's in all clinical data columns for Control samples.

```{r}
final_pam50_filtered <- left_join(proteomes_pam50_transposed,
                                  clinical,
                                  by = c("patient_id" = "Complete TCGA ID")
                                  )

head(final_pam50_filtered)
```

### Removing NA's

#### From PAM50 set

```{r}
pam50_filtered_without_NA <- final_pam50_filtered |> 
  select(-(where(anyNA) & !starts_with("PAM50")))

head(pam50_filtered_without_NA)
```

#### From whole proteome set

```{r}
all_genes_without_NA <- final_dataset_all_genes |> 
  select(-(where(anyNA) & !starts_with("PAM50")))

head(all_genes_without_NA)
```

### Save the final tibbles as tsv files in the data folder

```{r}
write_tsv(x = pam50_filtered_without_NA, 
          file = str_c(data_path, "02_dat_clean_pam50_filtered_without_NA.tsv"))
```

```{r}
write_tsv(x = all_genes_without_NA, 
          file = str_c(data_path, "02_dat_clean_all_genes_without_NA.tsv"))
```
